title: Chronic Stress
subtitle: When repeated demand reshapes regulation
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating chronic stress across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain chronic stress in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in chronic stress.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to chronic stress.

sections.explainSimply: Chronic stress keeps protective systems active too often or for too long.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Repeated activation can alter sleep, attention, emotion regulation, immune signalling and learning while increasing avoidance and exhaustion.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Allostatic load describes cumulative regulatory cost, but it is a population-level construct rather than a clinical diagnostic test.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of chronic stress as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need chronic stress to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not attribute every symptom to cortisol or “nervous-system dysregulation.”
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use chronic stress to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses chronic stress to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not attribute every symptom to cortisol or “nervous-system dysregulation.” Evidence classification: established concept; individual effects vary.
